title: Grey shot 6 times, killed, during incident where police dog killed, officers cleared of wrongdoing
article: Law enforcement officials have been cleared of any wrongdoing during an incident June 17-18, 2021 where Lionel Ernest Grey, then 29, of Gift Lake, and police dog Jago, both died.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) launched an investigation into the matter and released its report Oct. 9, over three years later since the incident.
The report says that Grey died on the scene north of High Prairie after being shot six times.
"Death was due to multiple gunshot wounds," the report reads.
One officer fired five rounds, another six during the incident after Grey previously fired at officers.
Earlier, other officers shot at Grey during attempts to arrest him.
An autopsy on Grey showed that he had methamphetamine in his system at the time of death.

"On June 17, (Grey) had warrants out for his arrest. (Four officers, SO1, SO2, SO3 and WO3) tracked him into a forest after he abandoned his vehicle. In the dense forest, (Grey) shot at the officers in an apparent attempt at an ambush, killing a police dog. SO2 responded by shooting back at (Grey). (Grey) ran away uninjured, and then circled back toward the officers. SO1 and SO3, when they spotted (Grey) coming back, fired at him.

"In the early morning of June 18, SO4, SO5, SO6, and WO4 (other officers) tracked (Grey) again. When they found him and he did not immediately surrender, SO4, SO5 and SO6 fired at him. (Grey) again escaped. Later that day, SO7 and SO8 (Other officers) were driving near the spot (Grey) was seen last and saw him on the side of the road. When he was told he was under arrest (Grey) picked up a rifle, SO7 and SO8 shot him.

"As noted above, defences under Section 25 and Section 34 of the Criminal Code are likely to apply to the actions of the subject officers. There are therefore no reasonable grounds to believe that the subject officers committed any offences."

In short, Section 25 of the Criminal Code allows officers to administer the law if he/she acts on reasonable grounds, justified in doing what he/she is required or authorized to do and in using as much force as is necessary that purpose.
In short, Section 34 of the Criminal Code cites everyone who is unlawfully assaulted without having provoked the assault is justified in defending themselves.
The report was issued by Matthew Block, assistant executive director, ASIRT.
